source_text: Num ergo et Apostolorum litterae mobiles? et nos usquequaque simplices animae, et solummodo columbae, libenter errantes? credo vivendi cupiditate. Ita vero sit, ut recedant a litteris suis sensus. Quae tamen passos Apostolos scimus, manifesta doctrina est; hanc intelligo solam Acta decurrens; nihil quaero; carceres illic, et vincula, et flagella, et saxa, et gladii, et impetus Judaeorum, et coetus nationum, et tribunorum elogia, et regum auditoria, et proconsulum tribunalia, et Caesaris nomen interpretem non habent. Quod Petrus caeditur, quod Stephanus opprimitur, quod Jacobus immolatur, quod Paulus distrahitur, ipsorum sanguine scripta sunt. Et si fidem Commentarii voluerit haereticus, instrumenta imperii loquentur, ut lapides Jerusalem. Vitas Caesarum legimus; orientem fidem Romae primus Nero cruentavit. Tunc Petrus ab altero cingitur, cum cruci adstringitur. Tunc Paulus civitatis romanae consequitur nativitatem, cum illic martyrii renascitur generositate. Haec ubicumque jam legero, pati disco; nec mea interest quos sequar martyrii magistros, sensusne an exitus Apostolorum; nisi quod et sensus in exitibus recognosco. Nihil enim passi fuissent, quod non prius patiendum esse sensissent. Cum vincula Paulo Agabus gestu quoque prophetasset, discipuli flentes et orantes ne se Jerosolyma committeret, frustra oraverunt. Ille enim, quod semper docuerat animatus: Quid fletis, inquit, et contristatis cor meum? At ego non modo vincula Jerosolymis pati optaverim, verum etiam mori pro nomine Domini mei Jesu Christi. Atque ita cesserunt, dicendo: Fiat voluntas Domini; fidentes scilicet, passiones ad voluntatem Dei pertinere. Non enim dehortationis consilio, sed dilectionis retinere tantaverant, ut Apostolum desiderantes, non ut martyrium dissuadentes. Quod si jam tunc Prodicus aut Valentinus assisteret, suggerens, non in terris esse confitendum apud homines; minus vero, ne Deus humanum sanguinem sitiat, nec Christus vicem passionis, quasi et ipse de ea salutem consecuturus exposcat; statim audisset a servo Dei, quod audierat a Domino diabolus: Recede, Satana, scandalum mihi es; scriptum est: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies. Sed et nunc audire debebit, quatenus multo post, venena ista suffudit; nulli infirmorum facile nisi nocitura, si qui non hanc nostram ex fide praebiberit, vel etiam superbiberit potionem.
pass_a_gloss: Are therefore also the letters of the Apostles changeable? And are we everywhere simple souls, and only doves, gladly wandering in error? I believe it is due to a desire to live. So indeed let it be, that the meanings depart from their letters. Which things we know the Apostles suffered, is a manifest doctrine; I understand this alone by running through the Acts; I seek nothing; the prisons, and the chains, and the whips, and the stones, and the swords, and the attacks of the Jews, and the gatherings of the nations, and the speeches of the tribunes, and the audiences of the kings, and the tribunals of the proconsuls, and the name of Caesar do not have an interpreter. That Peter is struck, that Stephen is overpowered, that James is slain, that Paul is torn apart, these things are written in their own blood. And if a heretic wishes to have faith in the Commentaries, the instruments of the empire will speak, like the stones of Jerusalem. We read the Lives of the Caesars; Nero first bloodied the rising faith at Rome. Then Peter is girded by another, when he is bound to the cross. Then Paul obtains the birth of the Roman city, when he is reborn there by the nobility of martyrdom. These things, wherever I now read, I learn to suffer; nor is it my concern whom I follow, the teachers of martyrdom, whether the meanings or the outcomes of the Apostles; except that I also recognize the meanings in the outcomes. For they would not have suffered anything that they had not previously sensed was to be suffered. When the chains of Paul were also prophesied by Agabus with a gesture, the disciples weeping and praying that he not commit himself to Jerusalem, prayed in vain. For he, inspired by what he had always taught, said: Why do you weep and sadden my heart? But I not only wish to suffer chains in Jerusalem, but also to die for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ. And so they yielded, saying: Let the will of the Lord be done; certainly trusting that the passions pertain to the will of God. For they had attempted to restrain him not with the counsel of dissuasion, but with the bond of love, so that they might retain the Apostle, desiring him, not dissuading him from martyrdom. But if then Prodicus or Valentinus had been present, suggesting that one should not confess on earth among men; much less, that God thirsts for human blood, nor that Christ, as if He Himself were going to obtain salvation from it, demands the substitute of passion; immediately he would have heard from the servant of God what he had heard from the Lord, that the devil said: Depart, Satan, you are a scandal to me; it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only. But also now he ought to hear, insofar as he much later poured out those poisons; none of the weak ones will easily drink, unless they have previously drunk or even drunk excessively this our potion of faith.

pass_b_english: Are the Apostles' letters also changeable? Are we everywhere simple souls, mere doves, gladly wandering in error? I believe it comes from a desire to live. So let it be, then: let the meanings depart from their letters. What we know the Apostles suffered is a manifest doctrine; I grasp it simply by reading through Acts; I seek nothing else. Prisons, chains, whips, stones, swords, Jewish attacks, mob gatherings, tribunals' speeches, royal audiences, proconsular courts, the very name of Caesar — none of these need an interpreter. That Peter was struck, that Stephen was crushed, that James was slain, that Paul was torn apart — these things were written in their own blood. And if a heretic wants to trust the Commentaries, the instruments of empire will speak, like the stones of Jerusalem. We read the Lives of the Caesars; Nero first bloodied the rising faith at Rome. Then Peter was girded by another when he was bound to the cross. Then Paul obtained the birth of the Roman city when he was reborn there through the nobility of martyrdom. Wherever I read these things now, I learn to suffer; it does not matter which teachers of martyrdom I follow, whether the meanings or the outcomes of the Apostles — except that I also recognize the meanings in the outcomes. For they would not have suffered anything that they had not first sensed was to be suffered. When Agabus also prophesied Paul's chains by a gesture, the disciples wept and prayed that he not commit himself to Jerusalem; they prayed in vain. For he, driven by what he had always taught, said: "Why do you weep and sadden my heart? But I not only wish to suffer chains in Jerusalem, but also to die for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ." And so they yielded, saying: "Let the will of the Lord be done"; certainly trusting that sufferings pertain to the will of God. For they had attempted to restrain him not with the counsel of dissuasion, but with the bond of love, so that they might retain the Apostle — desiring him, not dissuading him from martyrdom. But if Prodicus or Valentinus had been present then, suggesting that one should not confess on earth among men; much less that God thirsts for human blood, nor that Christ, as if He Himself were going to obtain salvation from it, demands the substitute of passion — immediately he would have heard from the servant of God what he had heard from the Lord the devil say: "Depart, Satan, you are a scandal to me; it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only" (Matthew 4:10). But also now he ought to hear, insofar as he much later poured out those poisons; none of the weak will easily drink them unless they have previously drunk — or even drunk excessively — this our potion of faith.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances (e.g., 'animatus' as 'inspired' vs 'driven'). Pass B correctly identifies the scripture citation (Matthew 4:10) which was alluded to in the Latin. The title 'Martyrdom of the Apostles' correctly names the thought of the passage.
